clues.title: Bollard: Bollard
text: Half-circle/flat curved shape bollards with a rectangular reflector on the front and two circular reflectors on the back are common. The reflectors can be white or orange, and sometimes these bollards have numbers on them.
Estonian bollards might look similar, but they have a rounded shape and will never have numbers on them.

clues.title: Street sign: Street name ending - iela
text: The Latvian word for street is "iela." This word is unique to Latvian, so if you see a street sign with it, you can be sure you're in Latvia.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: Hook pole
text: Wooden poles with alternating pattern of hook-shaped insulators are really common in Latvia. They might appear sometimes in other countries but if you see them with flat landscape you gonna be most likely in Latvia(If you vibe baltics). Always try using other clues to confirm it.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Long Leg Latvia
text: You can identify Latvia from their guy with weirdly **long legs**. Long as hell for what. It's arguable Russia/Ukraine/Lithuania has long legs but even so they have 3 zebra stripes, not 5.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Bollard: Bollards
text: Latvian bollards have a **thin**, **slightly curved** shape.

They have a rectangular reflector on the front, and two circular reflectors on the back. The reflectors can be white or orange. The black strip is slightly angled. Bollards often have numbers below the front reflector.
**NOTE:** Estonian and Lithuanian bollards look different.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: Pole Top
text: Latvian poles have distinctive poletops, with **hook-shaped insulators**, that are arranged in an **alternating** manner: left-right-left (or vice versa).
**NOTE:** These poletops are much more rare in the other two Baltic countries. They can however appear in some other European countries.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Stop sign: Bus Stop
text: Latvian bus stop signs have this design.
Most importantly, the bus has **five windows**. Within the Baltics, this is unique to Latvia. The other two Baltic countries have **four windows**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Sign: Sign Border
text: Each Baltic country has a slightly different border for its warning and speed signs.
Latvian signs have a **thick red border**, with a thin white outline around it.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pedestrian sign: Pedestrian Signs
text: Latvian pedestrian signs have **five stripes**, which is unique within the Baltics. Uniquely, the pedestrian has noticeably long legs compared to pedestrian signs in other European countries.
The other two Baltic countries have three stripes on their pedestrian signs.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: KM Marker
text: All Baltic countries use the same blue kilometre marker. However, they can be distinguished from each other by their angle relative to the road.
In Latvia, the marker will be **parallel** to the road. It only has a number on one side.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: White Bricks & Corrugated Roofs
text: Latvian architecture generally consists of a combination of wood and white brick, typically with somewhat steep corrugated metal roofs.
Slightly modern houses with pastel coloured stone walls and houses with a combination of wood with another material, particularly white brick, are also common.

clues.title: Language: Latvian
text: Latvian is a Baltic language closely related to Lithuanian. Within the Baltic languages, the following letters are unique to Latvian:
Vowels with a macron (horizontal stripe): **Ā Ē Ī** (both Latvian and Lithuanain use **Ū** however).
Consonants with a small hook: **Ģ Ķ Ļ Ņ** (Lithuanian has similar hooks connected to the bottom of vowels).
The Latvian word for street is **iela**. This word is unique to Latvian.
NOTE: Estonian is not a part of the Baltic language family (despite the name), but rather a Finnic language related to Finnish.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
